mainTopic: Found deeds of gift (בריא versus שכיב מרע, giver versus son) and a found שובר for a כתובה
overview: Our משנה implies that a found שטר מתנה (deed of gift) is handed over if the giver says 'Give it.' A ברייתא says not to hand it over even when both sides agree. The גמרא first answers that the משנה is about a שכיב מרע and the ברייתא is about a בריא. A שכיב מרע can always take back his gift, so if he made a later gift, the later deed wins (בתרא זכי) and returning the old deed hurts no one. A בריא cannot take back his gift, so the earlier delivered deed wins (קמא זכי). He might falsely claim that an old, never-delivered deed was handed over, just to undo a real later gift, so he is told to write a new deed instead. רב זביד objects that both sources speak of wills, which only a שכיב מרע makes. He answers that the משנה is when the dying giver himself asks, and the ברייתא is when his son asks after the father's death, since the son might be scheming to cancel his own binding gift. The גמרא then quotes a ברייתא about a found שובר (receipt) for a כתובה. It asks whether an early-dated receipt could let the husband cheat people who bought the wife's כתובה. רבא begins to answer, and his answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Splitting the two sources: healthy giver versus deathbed giver
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא settles the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא by saying each one is talking about a different kind of giver.
steps.simpleTranslation: This source is about a healthy person, and that source is about a person on his deathbed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction it just raised. One source is about a gift from a בריא, and the other is about a gift from a שכיב מרע. The next lines will spell out which source matches which case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה implies 'if he says give, the finder gives,' while the ברייתא says 'even if he says give, don't give.' Instead of picking one, the גמרא shows they are not arguing at all. They describe two different kinds of giver, whose gifts work differently.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This one... and that one': the standard way to split two sources into two different cases
A person who is dangerously ill, on his deathbed
A written deed that gives a gift

steps.confusionAlert: This line alone does not say which source is which. The very next step tells you that the משנה is the שכיב מרע case.

phrases.english: This one is about a healthy person,
phrases.notes: 'This one' and 'that one' point back to the משנה and the ברייתא that were just set against each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא raised just before this passage.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the sources into two different cases (healthy giver versus deathbed giver)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and the ברייתא seemed to disagree about whether a found deed of gift is handed over when the giver says 'give.'
steps.terutzMaskana: They do not disagree. Each one is talking about a different kind of giver.

steps.title: The משנה is about a deathbed giver, who can take his gift back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא assigns the משנה's rule ('if he says give, we give') to a שכיב מרע, because he is able to retract his gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our משנה, which implies that if he says 'give it' we give it, is about a person on his deathbed, because he is someone who can take back his gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains which source is the deathbed case: the משנה. The reason is that a שכיב מרע can always change his mind about his gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A gift from a שכיב מרע is never final while he is alive, so he can take it back. That fact will make handing over the found deed safe, as the next steps show.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Give it!' (the giver tells the finder to hand the deed over)
We give it (the finder hands it over)
Able to go back on, to retract

phrases.english: Our משנה, which teaches:
phrases.notes: The משנה never says this outright. It says not to return the deed because the giver may have changed his mind, so if he says 'give it,' he clearly hasn't.

phrases.english: but if he said 'Give it,' we give it,
is about a person on his deathbed, since he is someone who can retract.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fills in the answer from step 1 by naming the משנה as the שכיב מרע case and giving the reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's rule that the deed is handed over when the giver says 'give' applies to a שכיב מרע, because his gift can always be retracted.

steps.title: The worry: maybe he is secretly undoing a later gift
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises the possible concern about handing over the deed. Maybe the giver wrote this deed, never gave it, gave his property to someone else, and now wants to use the old deed to cancel that later gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: For we say: what could be the problem? Perhaps he first wrote the deed for this person, changed his mind, and did not give it to him. Then he wrote a deed for someone else and gave it to him. Now he is going back on the gift he gave that other person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lays out the worry someone might have about handing over the found deed. This is a setup: the next step shows why the worry is not a real problem in the שכיב מרע case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fear is a trick. The giver might use an old, never-delivered deed to undo a real gift he later gave to a second person. The phrase 'מאי איכא למימר' ('what is there to say?') tells us the גמרא is about to show this fear has no force here.

keyTerms.meaning: 'What is there to say?': what possible problem could there be?
He goes back on it, he retracts

phrases.english: For we say: what is there to worry about?
Perhaps he first wrote it for this person,
phrases.notes: 'This person' is the one named in the found deed.

phrases.english: then changed his mind and did not give it to him,
and then wrote it for another person
and gave it to him;
and now he is going back on his word
to that one whom he gave it to.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the שכיב מרע case is safe by first stating the worry that would otherwise stop us from handing over the deed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is there any risk that handing over the found deed lets the giver unfairly cancel a later gift he gave to someone else?

steps.title: No harm done: when two deeds appear, the later one wins
steps.stepSummary: The later recipient loses nothing. When both deeds come out, the later deed takes the property, because it shows the giver took back the first gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he gave it to him as a healthy person's gift, that person has no loss. When the two deeds come out, the later one acquires, because the giver clearly went back on the first one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the worry from step 3. The second recipient is safe, because the later deed always beats the earlier one here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first deed came from a שכיב מרע, and his gifts can be retracted. Writing a new deed for someone else shows he retracted the first one. So handing the old deed to its owner cannot hurt the later recipient, and the finder may give it when told to.

keyTerms.meaning: A gift given by a healthy person

steps.whatToRemember: In the משנה's case (a שכיב מרע), the finder may hand over the deed when the giver says 'give,' because any later deed would win anyway. The giver's power to retract protects the later recipient.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a general rule for deathbed gifts. Since they can be retracted, a later conflicting gift beats an earlier one, so the order of the deeds decides who gets the property.

phrases.english: If he gave it to him as a healthy person's gift,
he has no loss,
because when the two come out,
phrases.notes: 'The two' are the two deeds, shown together in בית דין.

phrases.english: the later one acquires,
since he clearly went back on the first one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בְּמַתְּנַת בָּרִיא יַהֲבַהּ לֵיהּ – לֵית לֵיהּ פְּסֵידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the worry raised in step 3 and completes the explanation of the משנה as the שכיב מרע case.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The later recipient loses nothing. When both deeds come out, the later deed acquires, because the giver retracted the first one.

steps.title: Even a later deathbed gift loses nothing
steps.stepSummary: The answer from step 4 also covers the case where the second gift was given as a מתנת שכיב מרע: the later recipient still wins.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if he gave it to the second person as a deathbed gift, that person loses nothing. The later deed acquires, because the giver has backed out of the first gift.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to the worry from step 3. Even if the second gift was a deathbed gift, the second recipient loses nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שכיב מרע can always take back his gifts. So when two of his deeds appear, the later one shows he changed his mind about the earlier one. Returning the old deed therefore cannot hurt the later recipient.

keyTerms.meaning: a gift made by a person on his deathbed

steps.whatToRemember: With a שכיב מרע, the LATER deed wins, because he is always able to change his mind.

phrases.english: If as a deathbed gift
he also gave it to him (the second person),
there is no loss in it –
because the later one acquires,
since he is backing out of the first one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי בְּמַתְּנַת שְׁכִיב מְרַע נָמֵי יַהֲבַהּ נִיהֲלֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the answer of step 4 to the case where the second gift was also a deathbed gift.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The later deathbed gift overrides the earlier deed, so returning the earlier deed causes no harm.

steps.title: The ברייתא is talking about a healthy giver
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's rule, that the deed is returned to neither party even if both agree, is placed in the case of a בריא, who cannot take back his gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the ברייתא teaches that even if both agree, he should not return it to either one, it is talking about a healthy person, who is not able to retract.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the answer from step 1. The גמרא places the ברייתא's strict rule in the case of a healthy giver.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 put the משנה with a שכיב מרע, who can change his mind. Here the ברייתא is put with a בריא, who cannot. That difference is why returning the deed is safe in one case and risky in the other.

keyTerms.meaning: someone able to retract (take back a gift)

phrases.english: When it teaches in the ברייתא:
Even though both of them agree
phrases.notes: Both the giver and the person named in the deed agree that it is real.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַחְזִיר לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה –
phrases.english: he should not return it, neither to this one nor to that one –
that is about a healthy person, who is not able to retract,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the answer of step 1 and applies its second half to the ברייתא, parallel to step 2's handling of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא's ban on returning the deed applies to a gift from a healthy person, who cannot retract.

steps.title: The danger: a healthy giver using an old deed to undo a real gift
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the worry. A healthy giver may have given the property to someone else, and now wants the old, earlier-dated deed returned so that it beats the later gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: We say: perhaps he first wrote the deed for this person, changed his mind and did not give it, then wrote one for another person and gave it to him. Now he wants to back out of that real gift. He thinks: 'I can't legally retract, so I'll tell the court I gave it to this one, they'll give him the deed, and when he shows it, its earlier date will win.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the deed of a healthy giver is not returned. He might be trying to trick the court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בריא cannot take back a gift, so the first deed actually delivered wins, not the later one. A giver who regrets a real gift could claim that his old, never-delivered deed was delivered. Its earlier date would then wrongly push out the true recipient.
steps.confusionAlert: With a שכיב מרע the LATER deed wins. With a בריא the EARLIER delivered deed wins. That flip is the whole reason the two cases are treated differently.

phrases.english: For we say: perhaps he wrote it for this one at first
and changed his mind and did not give it to him,
and then he wrote it for another person
and gave it to him –
now he wants to back out
from that one to whom he gave it

phrases.aramaic: וְסָבַר: מִהְדָּר לָא מָצֵינָא הָדַרְנָא בִּי,
phrases.english: and he thinks: I am not able to retract outright,
I will tell them that I gave it to this one,
and they will return the deed to him,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּכִי מַפֵּיק הַאי כְּתָבָא,
phrases.english: so that when he brings out this deed,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind step 6: why a healthy giver's deed is not returned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A healthy giver might falsely claim delivery of an old deed so that its earlier date overrides a real later gift.

steps.title: The court refuses to hand over the old deed
steps.stepSummary: The court tells the healthy giver it will not give the found deed to the person named in it, because the giver may be trying to undo a gift he really made to someone else.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we say to him: we will not give this deed to this person. Perhaps you wrote it but never gave it to him, then gave the property to someone else, and now you are trying to back out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now tells us what the court actually says to the giver. It refuses to return the old deed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court openly tells the giver its suspicion: the deed may have been written but never handed over. Even though giver and recipient agree, the court protects an unknown third person who may have received a real gift.

keyTerms.meaning: you did not give it (hand it over)

phrases.english: Rather, we say to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the giver. The court is speaking.

phrases.aramaic: הַאי כְּתָבָא לָא יָהֲבִינַן לֵיהּ לְהַאי.
phrases.english: This deed we will not give to this one.
Perhaps you did write it,
but you did not give it to him,
and you gave it to another person
and now you are backing out of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the worry from step 7 into the court's practical response: refusal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The court does not return a healthy giver's found deed, even when both sides agree.

steps.title: The fix: write a brand-new deed
steps.stepSummary: If the giver really wants this person to have the gift, he should write a new deed now. That is safe, because if he gave the property to someone else earlier, that earlier recipient still wins.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you did not give it to another person and you want to give it to this one, write him another deed now and give it to him. Then, if you did give it to another person, he loses nothing, because the earlier one acquires.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends with practical advice for the honest giver: write a new deed with today's date.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A new deed carries a new, later date. For a בריא the earlier delivered gift wins, so any real earlier recipient stays protected. An honest giver loses nothing by writing a new deed, and a dishonest one gains nothing.
steps.whatToRemember: משנה (return the deed) = שכיב מרע, where the later deed wins, so returning it is harmless. ברייתא (don't return) = בריא, where the earlier deed wins, so returning it could be a trick. The healthy giver's solution is to write a new deed.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key principle: the court will not let a document's early date be used to hurt a third party who may have a real claim. It always looks for a way that protects everyone.

phrases.english: If you did not give it to another person
and you want to give it to this one,
write him now another deed
and give it to him,
so that if you did give it to another person
there is no loss in it, because the earlier one acquires.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the court's statement from step 8 by giving the honest giver a safe way forward.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A healthy giver's found deed is not returned. If he truly wants to give the gift, he writes a new deed, which cannot harm any earlier real recipient.

steps.title: רב זביד: Both Sources Talk About Wills
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד challenges the earlier answer. Both the משנה and the ברייתא speak about דייתיקאות (wills of a dying person), so the ברייתא cannot be about a בריא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד objects: But both the משנה and the ברייתא are teaching about wills!
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד attacks the answer from the earlier steps, which said the ברייתא is about a healthy giver (בריא).
steps.deeperAnalysis: A דייתיקי is the will of a שכיב מרע, a person on his deathbed. Since the ברייתא uses that same word, it cannot be talking about a healthy person. So the earlier way of splitting the two sources does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it (a strong challenge to an earlier answer)
Both this one and that one
Wills: gift documents of a person on his deathbed

phrases.english: Rav Zevid objects to this:
But both this and that
phrases.notes: He means both the משנה and the ברייתא.

phrases.english: are teaching about wills!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the claim that the ברייתא is about a בריא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא's case is a healthy giver.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says דייתיקאות, and that word only fits a שכיב מרע, so it cannot be about a בריא.

steps.title: רב זביד's New Answer: The Giver Versus His Son
steps.stepSummary: Both sources are about a שכיב מרע. The משנה is when the giver himself says to return the deed; the ברייתא is when his son says so.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב זביד said: Both are about a dying person, and there is no contradiction. This one is about the giver himself, and that one is about his son.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד gives a new way to settle the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference is no longer healthy versus dying. Now it is about who is asking for the deed to be returned. If the giver himself asks, we return it. If his son asks after the giver died, we do not.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Zevid said:
Both this and that are about a person on his deathbed,
and it is not difficult:
this one is about him himself,
and that one is about his son!
phrases.notes: The father has died, and now the son is the one saying to return the deed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer with a new distinction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא) by who asks for the return
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two sources differ because one is about a בריא and one is about a שכיב מרע.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are about a שכיב מרע. The משנה is when the giver himself asks; the ברייתא is when his son asks.

steps.title: Why We Return the Deed When the Giver Himself Asks
steps.stepSummary: When the dying giver himself says 'give,' it is safe to return the deed, because he can retract. If he gave the property to someone else, the later gift wins.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה, which says that if he says 'give' we give, is about the giver himself, since he can retract. We say: even if he gave it to someone else, there is no loss, because when there is a first and a last gift, the last one wins, since he retracted from the first.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the משנה's side of רב זביד's answer: why returning the deed is safe when the giver himself asks for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שכיב מרע can always take back his gift. If he made a later gift to someone else, that later gift beats the old deed. So handing over the old deed cannot hurt anyone.

keyTerms.meaning: Give! (the giver's instruction to return the deed)
Someone who is able to retract
The first and the last (two gifts)

phrases.english: That which says, "If he says 'give,' we give,"
is about the giver himself,
since he is someone who can retract,
for we say:
even if he gave it to another person,
there is no loss in it,
because when there is a first and a last,
the last one acquires,
since he has retracted from the first.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first half of רב זביד's answer (the משנה).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the dying giver himself asks, the deed is returned, because a later gift from him would beat it anyway.

steps.title: The ברייתא's Case Is the Son
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's rule, not to return the deed even if both sides agree, is about a case where the son is the one agreeing.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the ברייתא teaches that even though both of them agree, he should not return it to either one, it is about his son.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא places the ברייתא's strict rule in the case where the giver has died and his son agrees to return the deed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if both 'sides' agree, here those sides are the son and the person named in the deed, not the father. The next step explains why the son's agreement is not trusted.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה

phrases.english: When it teaches in the ברייתא:
"Even though both of them agree,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַחְזִיר לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה,
phrases.english: he should return it neither to this one nor to that one,"
that is about his son.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second half of רב זביד's answer (the ברייתא).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא's ruling not to return the deed applies when the son, not the father, approves the return.

steps.title: The Worry: The Father Changed His Mind and the Son Gave It Away
steps.stepSummary: Perhaps the father wrote the deed, changed his mind and never handed it over. Then, after the father died, the son gave the property to someone else, and now he wants to back out of that gift.
steps.simpleTranslation: For we say: Perhaps his father wrote it for this person, then changed his mind and did not give it to him. After his father died, the son wrote a deed for another person and gave it to him, and now he wants to back out from that person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining why the son's agreement is suspicious, by describing a possible hidden story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the father never handed over the deed, the father's gift never took effect, so the son inherited the property. The son then really gave it to someone else. Now he regrets that gift.

phrases.english: For we say:
perhaps his father wrote it for this one,
and then changed his mind and did not give it to him,
and after his father,
phrases.notes: He means after the father died.

phrases.english: he, the son, wrote it to another person
and gave it to him,
and now he is backing out from that one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind the ruling in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a real chance the son already gave the property away and is now trying to undo it.

steps.title: The Son's Scheme to Undo His Own Gift
steps.stepSummary: The son cannot legally take back his gift, so he plans to claim his father gave the deed. The father's earlier deed would beat the son's gift, and then he and the first person would split the property.
steps.simpleTranslation: He thinks: I cannot retract. I will tell the court that my father gave the deed to this person, and they will give him his document. Then he will go and take the property away from the other one, since he wins, and I will split it with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining the worry by spelling out the son's plan step by step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son is not a שכיב מרע, so he cannot simply cancel his gift. By getting the court to return his father's older deed, the person named in it would win over the son's later recipient. The son and that person would then share the property. This is why the ברייתא says not to return the deed.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב זביד, both sources are about a שכיב מרע. If the giver himself says 'give,' we return the deed, since any later gift of his still wins. If his son says 'give,' we don't, because the son may be using his father's old deed to cancel his own later gift.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key rule: a court will not hand over a document when doing so could help someone get around a gift he cannot legally take back.

phrases.english: He thinks:
"I cannot retract.
I will tell them
that my father gave it to this one,
and they will give him his document,
and he will go and take it away from him,
since he wins it,
phrases.notes: The father's gift comes before anything the son gave, so it beats the son's recipient.

phrases.english: and I will split it with him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation of the son's possible trick begun in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son might use his father's old deed to defeat his own binding gift and share the profit, so the deed is not returned.

steps.title: So we do not return the father's deed
steps.stepSummary: Because the son might be using the deed to undo his own gift, בית דין tells him it will not hand the deed over.
steps.simpleTranslation: Therefore we say to him: We will not give this deed to this person. Perhaps your father wrote it but never gave it, and then you gave the property to someone else, and now you want to back out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the practical conclusion from the worry raised in steps 14–15: בית דין refuses to hand over the found deed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son agrees the deed should be returned, but his agreement is suspicious. If the father never handed it over, the son's own later gift is valid, and the son cannot cancel it. Returning the old deed could let him cancel it by a trick, so the deed stays put.

keyTerms.meaning: A written document (here, the deed of gift)

phrases.notes: "Him" is the son, who agreed that the deed should be returned.

phrases.english: This deed we will not give to this person,
because perhaps his father did write it,
but he did not give it to him,
and you gave it to another person,
and now you are backing out of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical ruling from the suspicion described in step 15.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When only the son agrees, the found deed is not returned, so that he cannot use it to undo his own gift.

steps.title: The fix: the son should write a new deed
steps.stepSummary: If the son is honest, he can write a fresh deed himself. This cannot hurt anyone who already received the property from him, because an earlier deed beats a later one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if you are telling the truth that your father gave it to him, go now and write him another deed. Even if your father never gave it and you already gave the property to someone else, nobody loses, because between a first deed and a later one, the first one wins.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers the son an honest alternative: instead of returning the old deed, he should write a new one in his own name today.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A new deed from the son carries today's date. If the son already gave the property to someone else, that earlier gift still wins, so the other person is protected. If the son is sincere, the new deed lets him give the property to the first person without any trick.

keyTerms.meaning: The first and the later one

steps.whatToRemember: A found deed of a שכיב מרע is returned when the giver himself says so. It is not returned when only his son agrees, because of possible trickery. An honest son can simply write a new deed, since between the son's own gifts (which he cannot take back) the earlier one wins.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the flip side of the שכיב מרע rule. For gifts that cannot be taken back, קמא זכי: the earlier one takes the property. For a שכיב מרע, בתרא זכי. That is why a new deed from the son is safe while returning the father's old deed is dangerous.

phrases.english: Rather, if you are telling the truth
that your father gave it to him,
go yourself now
and write him another deed,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי נָמֵי לָא יַהֲבַהּ לֵיהּ אֲבוּהּ
phrases.english: for even if his father did not give it to him
and you wrote it over to another person,
there is no loss in it,
because when there is a first and a later one,
the first one acquires.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After refusing to return the old deed, the גמרא gives the son a safe way to carry out the gift.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The son should write a new deed. It cannot harm anyone who received the property from him earlier, because the earlier deed wins.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When only the son agrees, the father's found deed is not returned. An honest son writes a new deed himself, which cannot harm anyone who earlier received the property from him, because between his own competing gifts the first one wins.

steps.title: A ברייתא: finding a receipt for a כתובה payment
steps.stepSummary: If someone finds a שובר and the wife admits she was paid, he returns it to the husband. If she does not admit it, he gives it to neither of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If someone found a receipt, then when the wife admits it, he should return it to the husband. If the wife does not admit it, he should return it neither to this one nor to that one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a ברייתא about a lost שובר, the receipt a wife gives when her כתובה has been paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband needs the receipt to prove he already paid the כתובה. If the wife agrees she was paid, giving him the receipt seems safe. If she denies it, the finder cannot decide between them, so he holds onto it.

keyTerms.meaning: A receipt showing a debt or כתובה was paid
Neither to this one nor to that one

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If one found a receipt,
phrases.notes: This is the receipt a wife writes saying her כתובה was paid. The husband keeps it as proof.

phrases.english: when the wife admits it,
he should return it to the husband.
If the wife does not admit it,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַחְזִיר לֹא לָזֶה וְלֹא לָזֶה.
phrases.english: he should return it neither to this one nor to that one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from found deeds of gift to a new kind of found document, a receipt for a כתובה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A found שובר goes back to the husband if the wife admits it. If she denies it, it goes to neither side.

steps.title: But maybe she sold her כתובה before handing over the receipt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges returning the receipt even when the wife agrees. She might have written it in ניסן, kept it until תשרי, and sold her כתובה in between.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, when the wife admits it, he returns it to the husband. But let us worry: perhaps she wrote it to give in ניסן but did not give it until תשרי, and in the meantime she went and sold her כתובה for a small payment, between ניסן and תשרי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a challenge against the ברייתא: even the wife's agreement might not make it safe to return the receipt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A receipt dated ניסן makes it look as if the כתובה was paid off in ניסן. If she actually sold her כתובה rights after that date but before handing the receipt over, the husband could wrongly use the early date to defeat the buyer. This is the same worry as with the son: an old date can be used to undo a later deal.

keyTerms.meaning: The marriage contract a wife collects on divorce or widowhood
A small payment for a possible future benefit

steps.confusionAlert: The wife is not lying when she admits she was paid. The problem is the DATE on the receipt, which is earlier than the real handover and could hurt the buyer of her כתובה.

phrases.english: In any case, when the wife admits it,
he should return it to the husband.
But let us worry that perhaps she wrote it
to give it in ניסן,
and did not give it until תשרי,
and she went and sold her כתובה
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are added to correct the spelling of "her כתובה."

phrases.english: for a small payment
phrases.notes: The buyer pays a little now and collects the כתובה later, if she is ever divorced or widowed.

phrases.english: between ניסן and תשרי.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first ruling of the ברייתא quoted in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that a found שובר is returned to the husband when the wife admits it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A receipt dated earlier than its real handover could let the husband defeat someone who bought the wife's כתובה in between. So even her admission should not make returning it safe.

steps.title: The husband could use the early-dated receipt to cheat the buyers
steps.stepSummary: The challenge is completed. The husband could show the receipt dated ניסן and use it to wrongly take back from the people who bought the כתובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And then the husband will bring out the receipt that is dated ניסן, and he will come to take back from the buyers unfairly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the challenge it began in Step 19. It spells out exactly what harm could come from giving the receipt back to the husband.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose the wife wrote the receipt in ניסן but was not actually paid until תשרי, and in between she sold her כתובה to a buyer. When the buyer later collects, the husband could show the ניסן date and claim the wife had already been paid before she sold it. That would make the sale look worthless, so he could take back what the buyer collected, even though this is not fair.

keyTerms.meaning: To seize or take back property or money
Not according to the law; unfairly

steps.confusionAlert: The wife really was paid in the end. The problem is only the date. The receipt says ניסן, but the payment actually came later, after she had already sold her כתובה. The early date is what lets the husband cheat.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows why the date on a document matters so much. A receipt with a date that is too early can wipe out rights that other people got honestly in the meantime.

phrases.english: And he will bring out the receipt
phrases.notes: "He" is the husband. This happens after the buyer of the כתובה has already collected from him.

phrases.english: that is written in ניסן
and he will come to take back from the buyers
phrases.notes: The buyers are the people who bought the wife's כתובה between ניסן and תשרי.

phrases.english: unfairly

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the קשיא from Step 19 by stating the final harm: the husband could cheat the buyers.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling in Step 18 that the found שובר is returned to the husband when the wife admits she was paid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wife admitting she was paid does not prove the date on the receipt is true. An early date could let the husband undo a sale of the כתובה that was made in between, so returning the receipt could cause unfair loss to the buyers.

steps.title: רבא begins his answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces רבא, who will answer the challenge about the early-dated receipt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. It tells us that רבא is about to answer the challenge, and his actual words come on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the challenge says that returning the receipt could hurt the buyers of the כתובה. רבא's answer will explain how the ruling in Step 18 can still stand despite this worry. Nothing has been resolved yet, because only his name is introduced here.

keyTerms.meaning: A major אמורא (a sage of the גמרא) of Babylonia
Said; this introduces a sage's statement

phrases.english: רבא said:
phrases.notes: His actual answer continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces the response to the קשיא laid out in Steps 19-20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Answer not yet stated; it continues on the next amud.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The challenge assumes that returning the receipt to the husband exposes the buyers of the כתובה to unfair loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: Still to come: רבא's explanation of why the ruling in Step 18 is not undone by this worry.
